med-bias-01-c2.text: Matthew Gentzkow, Jesse M. Shapiro (2010). What Drives Media Slant? Evidence from U.S. Daily Newspapers. Econometrica 78(1), 35-71 (NBER Working Paper 12707).
med-bias-01-c2.quote: Our analysis confirms an economically significant demand for news slanted toward one's own political ideology.
med-bias-01-c2.claim: Most newspapers' slant matches the politics of their audiences, and Gentzkow and Shapiro's evidence suggests this is largely a market response rather than an ideological project.

med-bias-01-c2.text: Robert P. Vallone, Lee Ross, Mark R. Lepper (1985). The Hostile Media Phenomenon: Biased Perception and Perceptions of Media Bias in Coverage of the Beirut Massacre. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 49(3), 577-585.
med-bias-01-c2.quote: After viewing identical samples of major network television coverage of the Beirut massacre, both pro-Israeli and pro-Arab partisans rated these programs, and those responsible for them, as being biased against their side.
med-bias-01-c2.claim: Studies of the so-called hostile media effect (Vallone, Ross, and Lepper, 1985) show that partisans on opposite sides of an issue can both rate the same news report as biased against them

med-bias-01-c3.text: Bill Kovach, Tom Rosenstiel (2001). The Essence of Journalism Is a Discipline of Verification (excerpt from The Elements of Journalism). Nieman Reports, Nieman Foundation for Journalism at Harvard.
med-bias-01-c3.quote: In the original concept, in other words, the method is objective, not the journalist.
med-bias-01-c3.claim: Critics call it abandoned objectivity, while defenders argue it's the recovery of older norms (Kovach and Rosenstiel's "discipline of verification")
